mcqs.question: What does it mean for an exception to be 'precise'?
options: Every instruction before the faulting one has fully completed and none after it has started, giving a clean, well-defined stopping point
The exception handler always executes in exactly one clock cycle
The exception can only occur during the fetch stage
The CPU guarantees the exception will never repeat
mcqs.explanation: Precision is about a clean instruction-boundary stopping point — a prerequisite for the OS to inspect state and resume correctly. It has nothing to do with handler execution time, exceptions can be detected at various stages (not just fetch), and precision doesn't guarantee non-recurrence.

mcqs.question: Why is an invalid-opcode exception typically detected during decode rather than execute?
options: Because the ALU always detects invalid opcodes as part of computing overflow
Because decode is where the bit pattern is checked against known instruction encodings
Because decode happens after execute in the instruction cycle
Because invalid opcodes can only occur in memory instructions
mcqs.explanation: Decode is exactly where the hardware interprets the opcode field, so a pattern matching no known instruction is naturally caught there. The ALU's overflow flag is unrelated to opcode validity, decode occurs before execute (not after), and invalid opcodes can occur in any instruction type, not just memory ones.

mcqs.question: What's the key distinction between an interrupt and an exception?
options: Interrupts are internal to the executing instruction; exceptions come from external devices
There is no real distinction; the terms are interchangeable
Interrupts are external and asynchronous (e.g., a device signal); exceptions are internal and synchronous, tied to the currently executing instruction
Exceptions can only be caused by software, never by hardware
mcqs.explanation: Interrupts originate outside the current instruction stream and can occur at any time; exceptions are triggered by the instruction itself, synchronously. The first option reverses the actual definitions, the terms describe genuinely distinct concepts, and exceptions like divide-by-zero or page faults are triggered by hardware-detected instruction conditions, not purely software.

mcqs.question: What's the main advantage of vectored exception handling over a single-entry-point design?
options: It eliminates the need for any handler code at all
It requires less hardware than single-entry-point handling
It only works for interrupts, never for exceptions
The hardware jumps directly to a dedicated handler per exception type, avoiding a software dispatch step and reducing entry latency
mcqs.explanation: Vectored handling's dedicated per-type entry points skip a software dispatch/lookup step, lowering latency — valuable for time-sensitive interrupts. Handler code is still required either way, vectored handling applies to both interrupts and exceptions, and it typically needs more hardware (a vector table), not less.

mcqs.question: Why do deeply pipelined or out-of-order CPUs find it harder to guarantee precise exceptions?
options: Because multiple instructions are in flight at once, potentially completing out of program order, requiring hardware to unwind or suppress 'future' work before reporting an exception cleanly
Because such CPUs never actually generate exceptions
Because pipelining eliminates the concept of instruction boundaries entirely
Because precise exceptions are only a software-level concept, unaffected by pipelining
mcqs.explanation: With overlapping, possibly reordered instructions, hardware needs mechanisms (like reorder buffers) to present a clean boundary despite the underlying complexity. Exceptions certainly still occur in these CPUs, instruction boundaries still exist (they're just harder to expose cleanly), and precision is a hardware-level guarantee, directly affected by pipelining and out-of-order execution.

mcqs.question: Code briefly masks interrupts around a two-register hardware update that must appear atomic to any interrupt handler. Why doesn't this same trick protect against an incoming NMI?
options: NMIs are deliberately delivered regardless of the software interrupt mask, since they signal conditions considered too urgent to ever defer
NMIs are actually a subtype of maskable interrupt with a different name
The mask instruction only works on hardware built before 2010
NMIs never actually interrupt running code, only log an event for later
mcqs.explanation: Non-maskable interrupts exist specifically to bypass the software mask for urgent conditions like watchdog timeouts or uncorrectable memory errors — masking interrupts protects against ordinary maskable ones, but by design has no effect on an NMI. NMIs are a genuinely distinct category, not an older mask instruction quirk, and they do interrupt execution immediately rather than merely logging.
